source.title: Capturing Polysemanticity with PRISM: A Multi-Concept Feature Description Framework
source.authors: Laura Kopf; Nils Feldhus; Kirill Bykov; P. Bommer; Anna Hedstrom; M. Höhne; Oliver Eberle

record.tranche_reason: The study measures language-model feature polysemanticity using clustered activation examples, description embeddings and human judgments. This is a different method from the original vision-neuron examples.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports description-quality benchmarks, ablations of cluster size and text generators, and output-centric scores. Those results assess description methods rather than polysemanticity itself, so they are not recorded as rows here. Figure 3(b) reports polysemanticity scores only graphically; the text describes cross-model and layer patterns but gives no exact plotted values.
record.test_reason: The study measures the polysemanticity of MLP neurons in GPT-2 XL and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct (plus SAE features). It clusters top-activating text, generates five descriptions per neuron and scores their embedding similarity, with a small human check. This is a different method aimed at the same question as the originals. It does not test the claim in vision models and manipulates no mechanism.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that PRISM's multi-concept descriptions are more accurate than single-description methods, and that individual language-model features encode diverse, heterogeneous concepts. They report polysemanticity varies across models and feature types with no consistent layer trend. They find its polysemanticity scores align with human judgments in a small study (8 features, 7 participants).
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces a language-model method that samples high-activation text, clusters examples, generates multiple descriptions, and scores their semantic similarity. It does not reproduce the original vision-neuron analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Polysemanticity scores vary across models and feature types, with no consistent layer-depth trend. Description quality changes with the activation-percentile interval examined; alternative description/evaluation generators also change description-quality scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Residual-stream SAE features (GPT-2 Small, Gemma Scope) still carry diverse descriptions. Gemma Scope SAE features score most monosemantic across layers, and a GPT-2 Small SAE feature scores 0.30 (human 0.40).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE dictionary features in language models remain partly polysemantic, to a degree that varies by SAE.

fits_no_version.finding: Description quality (AUROC/MAD) of generated explanations falls when descriptions are built from lower activation-percentile intervals.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron explanation quality depends on which part of the activation range is sampled.

record.problems: The human evaluation uses only 8 features and 7 participants. PRISM fixes the number of clusters at 5 in its main setup, and the authors note that this may omit salient concepts. Polysemanticity scores are semantic similarity of generated descriptions rather than a direct causal test of shared or distinct underlying features. Figure 3(b) gives no exact score values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional direct polysemanticity results omitted. Description-quality comparisons between methods, text-generator ablations, cluster-size ablations, randomized-description AUROC/MAD checks, and output-centric faithfulness results were excluded because they do not directly measure the claim versions recorded here.

untested.parts: All of it: language models only, no image classifiers.
The share of MLP neurons that are polysemantic. There is no threshold or prevalence estimate; only 20 randomly chosen neurons per layer get mean similarity scores.
All of it: no capacity or superposition test.
All of it. No activation function, architecture or regularization is varied. The cross-model differences are uncontrolled and mix neurons with SAE features.
All of it. The study does not test whether diverse descriptions reflect one shared underlying feature.

Whether the polysemantic classification changes across activation-percentile intervals; only description quality was measured there. The effect of cluster count k on polysemanticity scores is also not reported.

missing.what: GPT-2 XL layer 47 neuron 3815, previously labelled possibly monosemantic, shown by PRISM to respond to multiple distinct concepts. This bears on method dependence of the polysemantic label.
Polysemanticity scores of true vs random descriptions by layer. Llama 3.1 8B MLP neuron descriptions approach the random baseline across layers, indicating widespread diversity.
Text statement that polysemanticity shows no consistent layer-depth trend for MLP neurons; rows r3-r8 lack it.
Human-study results for the other GPT-2 XL (layer 20, feature 3313) and Llama MLP neurons (layer 0, features 12733 and 10095).

record.verdict_notes: Primarily a feature-description method paper; much of the record measures PRISM's own description quality, which is not polysemanticity. Polysemanticity is operationalized as low embedding similarity among five LLM-generated cluster labels with k fixed at 5. This forces five clusters, so even monosemantic neurons get split; the score is relative and has no threshold for 'polysemantic'. SAE rows are relinked to none because V2 concerns MLP neurons. V5 is not tested because no architecture or training factor is varied.

versions.untested_parts: The study analyzes language models, not image classifiers or InceptionV1.

It does not estimate the share of MLP neurons that are polysemantic, or compare that share systematically across layers. The human study covers only a small set of features; it does not quantify unrelated token or context prevalence across a language model.
No capacity-pressure or superposition mechanism is manipulated or tested.
The study does not test initialization, regularization or training-noise explanations, or whether polysemanticity occurs without capacity pressure.

The paper compares polysemanticity scores across different models and feature types, but does not manipulate activation functions, architecture or regularization, nor show that polysemanticity can be lowered without a performance cost.
It does not establish whether apparently distinct concepts share a feature used by the model, or whether polysemantic neurons are actually detecting one common feature or related offshoots.
It tests how description quality changes across activation-percentile intervals, but does not report whether the classification or share of polysemantic neurons changes across those intervals.

tranche.reason: A different method (clustering plus multiple LLM descriptions plus a similarity score) aimed at whether LM neurons are polysemantic. It reports results for each layer and model, and a human check.

source_check.notes: The Section 4.4 sentence on 'no consistent trend across layers' pools all four models and feature types (two of them SAE sets). Per-model layer values are figure-only, except Llama, which A.6 says stays low across layers near the random baseline. The conclusion also claims PRISM captures 'differences in polysemanticity across model layers'. Layers: GPT-2 XL 0/20/40; Llama 0/20/30.

statements.problem: The PRISM part is right: one GPT-2 XL neuron, PRISM 0.38, human 0.40, lower means more polysemantic. It is one of 8 hand-picked human-study features. Seven participants, NeurIPS, code, controls and uncertainty all check out.
